question: What is C and what is it used for?
answer:
C is a procedural, compiled, low-level language created in 1972. It provides direct memory access via pointers and maps closely to machine operations.

Used for: operating systems (Linux kernel), embedded systems, device drivers, databases (PostgreSQL, Redis), language runtimes (Python interpreter, JVM), and performance-critical libraries.
tip: C is the foundation — most systems software and many languages are built on or influenced by C.
revise:
**C** = procedural, compiled, low-level language (1972) with direct memory access via pointers.
• Maps closely to machine operations → fast + predictable.
• Used for: OS kernels (Linux), embedded, drivers, databases (Postgres, Redis), language runtimes (CPython, JVM).
• **Interview tip**: it's the foundation — most systems software and many languages are built on or influenced by C.

question: What is a pointer in C?
answer:
A pointer is a variable that stores the memory address of another variable. Declared with *: int *p;

  • &x — address-of operator (get address of x).
  • *p — dereference (access value at address).

Pointers enable dynamic memory, arrays, strings, function callbacks, and efficient parameter passing by reference.
tip: Uninitialized pointers and dangling pointers are the #1 source of crashes in C.
deep:
Why pointers exist

C passes function arguments by value (copies). Pointers let you modify the caller's data, avoid copying large structs, and allocate memory that outlives the function.

Common pointer mistakes

  • NULL dereference — always check before use.
  • Dangling pointer — pointing to freed/stack memory.
  • Memory leak — malloc without free.
  • Buffer overflow — writing past array bounds.

How to say it in an interview

“A pointer stores an address. I use & to get an address and * to dereference. Pointers are essential for dynamic memory, passing by reference, and data structures — but they require careful lifetime and bounds management.”
revise:
A **pointer** = a variable holding another variable's **memory address** (declared `int *p`).
• `&x` = address-of; `*p` = dereference (value at that address).
• Enable dynamic memory, arrays, strings, callbacks, pass-by-reference.
• **Interview tip**: **uninitialized and dangling pointers are the #1 source of crashes** in C — always initialise, and NULL after free.

question: malloc, calloc, realloc, and free.
answer:
• malloc(size) — allocate uninitialized bytes on the heap. Returns void* or NULL on failure.
  • calloc(n, size) — allocate and zero-initialize n elements.
  • realloc(ptr, new_size) — resize existing allocation (may move memory).
  • free(ptr) — release heap memory. Must match every malloc/calloc/realloc.

Heap memory persists until freed — unlike stack variables that die when the function returns.
tip: After free(ptr), set ptr = NULL to prevent double-free bugs.
revise:
Heap allocation functions:
• **`malloc(size)`** — uninitialized bytes; returns `void*` or NULL.
• **`calloc(n,size)`** — zero-initialized.
• **`realloc(ptr,n)`** — resize (may move).
• **`free(ptr)`** — release; must match every alloc.
• Heap lives until freed (unlike stack, which dies at function return).
• **Interview tip**: after `free(ptr)` set `ptr = NULL` to prevent double-free / use-after-free.

question: Stack vs heap memory.
answer:
StackHeap
AllocationAutomatic (local variables)Manual (malloc/free)
LifetimeFunction scopeUntil freed
SpeedVery fastSlower
SizeLimited (~1-8 MB)Limited by RAM
FragmentationNonePossible
tip: Returning a pointer to a local stack variable is undefined behavior — the stack frame is destroyed.
revise:
**Stack vs Heap**.
• **Stack** — automatic (locals), function-scoped lifetime, very fast, small (~1–8MB), no fragmentation.
• **Heap** — manual (`malloc`/`free`), lives until freed, slower, RAM-limited, can fragment.
• **Interview tip**: **returning a pointer to a local stack variable is undefined behavior** — that stack frame is destroyed on return.

question: Relationship between arrays and pointers.
answer:
An array name decays to a pointer to its first element in most contexts. arr[i] is equivalent to *(arr + i).

Key differences: sizeof(arr) gives total array size; sizeof(ptr) gives pointer size (8 bytes on 64-bit). Arrays can't be reassigned; pointers can.
tip: When passing an array to a function, you lose the size — always pass the length as a separate parameter.
revise:
An **array name decays** to a pointer to its first element in most contexts.
• `arr[i]` ≡ `*(arr + i)`.
• But `sizeof(arr)` = whole array; `sizeof(ptr)` = 8 bytes; arrays can't be reassigned, pointers can.
• **Interview tip**: passing an array to a function loses its size (it decays to a pointer) — **always pass the length as a separate parameter**.

question: How are strings represented in C?
answer:
C has no built-in string type. Strings are null-terminated char arrays — the '\0' character marks the end.

Use string.h: strlen, strcpy, strncpy (safer), strcmp, strcat. Always ensure the destination buffer is large enough.
tip: strcpy is dangerous — prefer strncpy or snprintf to prevent buffer overflows.
revise:
C has **no string type** — strings are **null-terminated `char` arrays** (`'\0'` marks the end).
• `<string.h>`: `strlen`, `strcpy`/`strncpy`, `strcmp`, `strcat`.
• Destination buffer must be large enough (must include room for the `'\0'`).
• **Interview tip**: `strcpy` is dangerous — prefer **`strncpy`/`snprintf`** to avoid buffer overflows.

question: What is a struct?
answer:
A struct groups related variables under one type. Members are stored contiguously in memory (with possible padding for alignment).

Access with dot notation (s.field) or arrow (ptr->field) for pointers to structs.
tip: Structs are the foundation for custom data types in C — linked lists, trees, and records are all built from structs + pointers.
revise:
A **struct** groups related variables into one type.
• Members stored contiguously (with alignment **padding**).
• Access: `s.field`, or `ptr->field` for a pointer to struct.
• **Interview tip**: struct + pointers is the foundation of every custom data type in C — linked lists, trees, records all build from it.

question: What are function pointers?
answer:
A variable that stores the address of a function. Syntax: return_type (*name)(param_types).

Used for: callbacks (qsort comparator, signal handlers), plugin architectures, state machines, and implementing polymorphism-like behavior in C.
tip: typedef makes function pointer syntax readable: typedef int (*compare_fn)(const void*, const void*);
revise:
A **function pointer** stores a function's address: `return_type (*name)(params)`.
• Uses: callbacks (`qsort` comparator, signal handlers), plugins, state machines, C-style polymorphism.
• **Interview tip**: `typedef` makes the syntax readable — `typedef int (*compare_fn)(const void*, const void*);`.

question: C preprocessor directives.
answer:
• #include — paste header file contents (<> for system, "" for local).
  • #define — text substitution / macros.
  • #ifdef / #ifndef / #endif — conditional compilation (header guards).
  • #pragma once — non-standard but widely supported header guard.

Macros are processed before compilation — no type checking.
tip: Prefer inline functions over macros for type safety. Use include guards in every header.
revise:
The **preprocessor** runs before compilation (text substitution, no type checking).
• `#include` (`<>` system, `""` local), `#define` macros, `#ifdef`/`#ifndef`/`#endif` conditional compilation, `#pragma once`.
• **Interview tip**: prefer **inline functions over macros** for type safety, and put an **include guard in every header**.

question: static, extern, const, and volatile.
answer:
• static (variable) — persists between function calls; file scope if at file level.
  • extern — declares a variable defined elsewhere (shared across files).
  • const — read-only; compiler may place in read-only memory.
  • volatile — tells compiler the value may change unexpectedly (hardware registers, ISR). No optimization caching.
tip: static at file scope = internal linkage (not visible to other translation units).
code:
static int count = 0;  // persists between calls
void increment() { count++; }
revise:
Storage-class / qualifiers:
• **`static`** — persists between calls; at file scope = internal linkage.
• **`extern`** — declares a variable defined elsewhere (shared across files).
• **`const`** — read-only.
• **`volatile`** — value may change unexpectedly (hardware regs, ISRs) → no caching optimization.
• **Interview tip**: `static` at file scope hides a symbol from other translation units (internal linkage).

question: What is undefined behavior in C?
answer:
Behavior the C standard does not define — the program can do anything (crash, wrong result, appear to work). Common sources:

  • Dereferencing NULL or dangling pointers
  • Signed integer overflow
  • Buffer overflow / out-of-bounds access
  • Use after free
  • Uninitialized variables
  • Modifying a string literal
tip: UB is not just a crash — the compiler may optimize assuming UB never happens, making bugs invisible in debug builds.
code:
char *s = "hello";
s[0] = 'H';  // UB: string literals are read-only
revise:
**Undefined behavior (UB)** = the standard imposes no rules → anything can happen (crash, wrong result, 'works').
• Sources: NULL/dangling deref, signed overflow, out-of-bounds, use-after-free, uninitialized vars, modifying a string literal.
• **Interview tip**: the compiler **optimizes assuming UB never happens** — so bugs can vanish in debug and reappear in release. Use `-fsanitize`.

question: Bitwise operators in C.
answer:
• & AND — mask bits
  • | OR — set bits
  • ^ XOR — toggle bits
  • ~ NOT — flip all bits
  • << left shift — multiply by 2^n
  • >> right shift — divide by 2^n

Used for: flags, embedded registers, fast arithmetic, permission bitmasks.
tip: n & 1 checks if n is odd. n << 1 doubles n (for unsigned).
revise:
**Bitwise operators**:
• `&` AND (mask), `|` OR (set), `^` XOR (toggle), `~` NOT (flip all).
• `<<` left shift (×2ⁿ), `>>` right shift (÷2ⁿ).
• Uses: flags, hardware registers, permission bitmasks, fast arithmetic.
• **Interview tip**: `n & 1` tests odd/even; `n << 1` doubles (unsigned).

question: Recursion in C — how does it work?
answer:
A function calls itself with a smaller subproblem until a base case stops recursion. Each call pushes a new stack frame.

Risks: stack overflow on deep recursion (limited stack size). Tail recursion may be optimized by the compiler but isn't guaranteed in C.
tip: Every recursive function needs a clear base case — otherwise infinite recursion and stack overflow.
revise:
**Recursion** = a function calls itself on a smaller subproblem until a **base case**.
• Each call pushes a **stack frame**.
• Risk: **stack overflow** on deep recursion; tail-call optimization isn't guaranteed in C.
• **Interview tip**: every recursive function needs a clear base case — miss it and you get infinite recursion → stack overflow.

question: File I/O in C.
answer:
Use FILE* from stdio.h:

  • fopen(path, mode) — open ('r', 'w', 'a', 'rb').
  • fread/fwrite — binary I/O.
  • fgets/fprintf — text I/O.
  • fclose — always close; flush buffers.

Check return values — fopen returns NULL on failure.
tip: Always fclose in all code paths — use a goto cleanup pattern or wrap in a function.
revise:
File I/O uses **`FILE*`** from `<stdio.h>`.
• `fopen(path, mode)` ('r'/'w'/'a'/'rb'); `fread`/`fwrite` (binary), `fgets`/`fprintf` (text); `fclose` flushes+closes.
• `fopen` returns NULL on failure — check it.
• **Interview tip**: always `fclose` on **every** code path — a `goto cleanup` pattern makes that reliable.

question: Implement a singly linked list node in C.
answer:
A node is a struct with data and a pointer to the next node. The list is a pointer to the head node.

Operations: insert (head/tail), delete, search, traverse. Memory must be manually managed with malloc/free.
tip: Drawing pointers on paper is the fastest way to debug linked list code in interviews.
revise:
A **singly linked list node** = a struct holding `data` + a `next` pointer; the list is a pointer to head.
• Ops: insert (head/tail), delete, search, traverse — all via `malloc`/`free`.
• **Interview tip**: **draw the pointers on paper** — it's the fastest way to get insert/delete rewiring right in an interview.

question: enum and typedef.
answer:
enum — named integer constants. Compiler assigns sequential values unless specified. Improves readability over magic numbers.

typedef — creates an alias for an existing type. Simplifies complex types (especially function pointers and structs).
tip: Use enum for state machines and error codes. typedef struct { ... } Name; avoids writing 'struct' everywhere.
revise:
**`enum`** = named integer constants (sequential unless set) — beats magic numbers.
• **`typedef`** = an alias for a type; tidies complex types (function pointers, structs).
• **Interview tip**: use `enum` for state machines/error codes; `typedef struct { ... } Name;` lets you drop the `struct` keyword everywhere.

question: sizeof and struct padding.
answer:
sizeof returns the size in bytes of a type or variable. sizeof(arr)/sizeof(arr[0]) gives array length.

Structs may have padding — the compiler inserts unused bytes so members align to their natural boundaries (e.g. int on 4-byte boundary). Reordering members can reduce struct size.
tip: If sizeof(struct) seems too large, check member ordering — put largest members first to minimize padding.
code:
struct Bad  { char a; int b; };  // likely 8 bytes (3 padding)
struct Good { int b; char a; };  // likely 8 bytes (3 padding at end)
revise:
**`sizeof`** = size in bytes; `sizeof(arr)/sizeof(arr[0])` = array length.
• Structs get **padding** so members align to natural boundaries (int on 4-byte).
• Reordering members changes total size.
• **Interview tip**: if a struct seems too big, **put the largest members first** to minimize padding.

question: What is a void pointer?
answer:
void* is a generic pointer that can point to any data type. Cannot be dereferenced directly — must be cast to the correct type first.

Used in: malloc (returns void*), qsort/bsearch callbacks, generic data structures, and low-level system programming.
tip: malloc returns void* which implicitly converts to any pointer type in C (unlike C++).
revise:
**`void*`** = a generic pointer to any type.
• **Can't be dereferenced directly** — cast to the real type first.
• Uses: `malloc` return, `qsort`/`bsearch` callbacks, generic data structures.
• **Interview tip**: in **C**, `void*` implicitly converts to any pointer type (unlike C++, which needs an explicit cast).

question: Why do header files need include guards?
answer:
Without guards, including a header twice causes duplicate definition errors. Include guards prevent re-processing:

#ifndef FILE_H / #define FILE_H / ... / #endif or #pragma once.

Headers declare (function prototypes, types); source files (.c) define (implementations).
tip: One .c file per module + matching .h for public API is the standard C project structure.
revise:
**Include guards** stop a header being processed twice (which causes duplicate-definition errors).
• `#ifndef FILE_H / #define FILE_H / ... / #endif`, or `#pragma once`.
• Headers **declare** (prototypes/types); `.c` files **define** (implementations).
• **Interview tip**: standard C module layout = one `.c` per module + a matching `.h` for its public API.

question: What causes a segmentation fault and how do you debug it?
answer:
A segfault occurs when a program accesses memory it doesn't have permission to access. Common causes:

  • NULL pointer dereference
  • Buffer overflow
  • Use after free
  • Stack overflow (deep recursion)
  • Writing to read-only memory

Debug with: gdb (core dumps), Valgrind (memory errors), AddressSanitizer (-fsanitize=address).
tip: Compile with -g for debug symbols and -Wall -Wextra to catch warnings that become bugs.
code:
gcc -g -Wall -fsanitize=address -o app app.c
gdb ./app
# run, then: bt (backtrace on crash)
revise:
A **segfault** = accessing memory you don't have permission for.
• Causes: NULL deref, buffer overflow, use-after-free, stack overflow, writing to read-only memory.
• Debug with **gdb** (core dumps), **Valgrind**, **AddressSanitizer** (`-fsanitize=address`).
• **Interview tip**: compile with `-g` (symbols) and `-Wall -Wextra` — most segfault-causing bugs show up first as warnings.
